source_user: Write a concise runbook entry for an engineer investigating speculative decoding. Case variant 5: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Speculative decoding uses a draft model to propose tokens and a target model to verify them; speedup depends on acceptance rate and verification cost.
corrected_answer: Runbook: first pin the target and draft checkpoints, tokenizer, decoding rule, runtime, precision, hardware, cache policy, and offered load. Mechanism: the draft proposes a block and the target verifies it in parallelizable work, committing the accepted prefix and restarting at the first rejection. Boundary: speculative decoding is not automatically faster; acceptance rate, proposal length, draft overhead, target verification cost, queueing, and cache capacity determine end-to-end results. Measure proposed/accepted/committed tokens, correctness, stage and end-to-end p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput, queueing, memory headroom, and failures against a matched target-only baseline. Generalize only across tested model, workload, and load regimes.
risks: Low acceptance or draft overhead can erase or reverse speedup.
Unmatched decoding semantics or token accounting can make the comparison invalid.
Memory pressure, cache limits, batching, and queueing can change tail latency and throughput.
evidence_required: Record exact checkpoints, tokenizer, verification/acceptance rule, proposal length, precision, runtime, hardware, cache and scheduler settings.

Run repeated matched target-only and speculative trials across prompt/output lengths and offered loads; report token accounting, correctness, latency quantiles, throughput, queueing, memory, and failures.

source_user: Calculation case 1: a model has 24 layers, 2 KV heads, head dimension 64, sequence length 1024, and INT8 KV values. Estimate bytes for one request's K/V cache. Show the formula and report GiB.
source_assistant: Use 2 × layers × sequence_length × KV_heads × head_dim × bytes_per_value. Here this is 2 × 24 × 1024 × 2 × 64 × 1 = 6291456 bytes = 0.005859 GiB. This excludes allocator metadata and other runtime memory.
corrected_answer: Assumptions: the stated KV-head count is the number of stored K heads and V heads have the same shape; both K and V are stored for every layer and token, with 1 byte(s) per value (INT8), no quantization metadata or padding, and binary GiB = 2^30 bytes. Formula: 2 × layers × sequence_length × KV_heads × head_dim × bytes_per_value = 2 × 24 × 1024 × 2 × 64 × 1 = 6291456 bytes = 0.005859 GiB. This is only the payload estimate for one request; allocator alignment, scales/zero-points, page tables, fragmentation, temporary workspaces, activations, weights, and runtime overhead are excluded. Validate by inspecting allocated cache blocks and accounting for padding/metadata under the actual runtime; do not infer total device memory from this payload alone.
risks: Actual allocation may exceed the payload because of alignment, paging, metadata, quantization scales, fragmentation, or workspace.
The estimate is wrong if KV heads, precision, layer count, or cache layout differ from the stated assumptions.
Multiple sequences, batching, prefixes, and sliding-window or eviction policies change aggregate memory.
evidence_required: Confirm model architecture, cache layout, bytes per stored value, padding/page size, and quantization metadata in the runtime.
Measure allocated KV memory for one request and scale across sequence lengths and concurrency, recording non-KV memory and headroom.
